member.name: M:geoDC.UiDriver.ElementResolver.ResolveReady(System.String,System.String,System.Boolean,System.TimeSpan)
member.summary:
Resolves an element and then waits until it has been laid out: present in the tree, on screen, and with a non-degenerate bounding rectangle.
Existence alone is a weak readiness signal. WPF adds an element to the automation tree when it is created, which can be before measure and arrange. IsOffscreen and BoundingRectangle are only meaningful afterwards, so requiring both means the element occupies space on screen, which is what a script waiting to take a screenshot needs. It does not check whether the data inside has finished arriving. Content that animates or streams never settles, so a wait that required it to would hang.
Both phases share one budget, so this cannot take materially longer than .

member.name: M:geoDC.UiDriver.ElementResolver.WaitFor(System.String,System.String,geoDC.UiDriver.WaitConditions,System.TimeSpan)
member.summary:
Polls until the element identified by satisfies , returning its final observed state(s).
Unlike , absence is an ordinary observation here rather than an error: it is the goal of --gone, and for a state condition the element may simply not have appeared yet. A missing is treated the same way, since a closed popup takes its scope anchor with it. Every poll re-searches the tree instead of trusting a held handle: a removed element's handle is not guaranteed to fail fast, WPF can replace a control while the old handle stays readable, and a second match appearing mid-wait must still fail as ambiguous.
On timeout throws wait-timeout carrying the last observation as error.state.

member.name: T:geoDC.UiDriver.ForegroundGuard
member.summary:
Keeps a passive-launched app out of the developer's way across one UI driver step.
Opening a window without activation is not enough on its own. Steps can still pull the app forward: a UIA SetFocus fallback, a combo expand, a popup restoring keyboard focus, or a WebView2 chart claiming focus as it loads. Instead of handling each case, the guard notes who owned the foreground before the step, hands it back if the app took it, and puts the app's windows (including popups opened by the step) under everything else. Screenshots are unaffected, because PrintWindow captures occluded windows.
The guard only runs in passive sessions. An active launch may come forward and is never pushed back. Verbs that need the foreground (key) refuse to run in a passive session, so no step there has a legitimate reason to take it.

member.summary: Starts guarding a step, or returns null when the session is not passive.

member.name: M:geoDC.UiDriver.ForegroundGuard.End(System.String)
member.summary: Restores the foreground if the step took it, and sends the app's windows to the back.

member.name: M:geoDC.UiDriver.GeoDcSession.TopLevelWindows
member.summary:
All top-level windows of the geoDC process. This is the default search scope, so open typed popups are visible without flags. Main window first, then the rest in z-order.
The windows are enumerated through Win32 (see ), not by asking UIA for the desktop's children. The UIA route walks every window on the machine and costs 6-8 s per call, paid again by every verb that resolves a window. EnumWindows also returns owned windows directly, so there are no owner chains to walk. The desktop's UIA children are only the unowned windows, and every detached or immersive popup sets Owner, so that query alone finds only the main window while popups are open.

member.name: T:geoDC.UiDriver.ProcessWindows
member.summary:
Win32 enumeration of a process's visible top-level windows.
This exists to keep UIA off the hot path. Asking UIA for the desktop's children and filtering by process id makes the provider walk every top-level window on the machine, reading properties cross-process on each. That was measured at 6-8 seconds per call, paid again by every verb that resolves a window. EnumWindows answers the same question in-process in microseconds, and the handles it returns convert straight to automation elements via FromHandle, which is a single direct call rather than a search.

member.name: T:geoDC.UiDriver.WindowActivation
member.summary:
Brings another process's window to the foreground so SendInput keystrokes land in it.
UIA's SetFocus and a bare SetForegroundWindow are not enough here. Windows only lets the process that already owns the foreground hand it over, and the UI driver is a console process launched from a terminal that keeps it. Attaching this thread's input queue to the current foreground thread (and to the target's) lifts that restriction for the duration of the call. This is the standard workaround. Without it the UI driver could only type into a window it had been handed the foreground for.
